summary:
High in the rocky grasslands of central Brazil, *Canthon corpulentus* — a small dung beetle of the family Scarabaeidae — made its home among the ancient, shallow soils of the campo rupestre. Known from only a handful of scattered localities above 1,000 meters, this rotund beetle was part of one of the world's most species-rich grassland ecosystems, quietly fulfilling its vital role in nutrient cycling across the highlands of Minas Gerais, Mato Grosso, and beyond.

Its survival now hangs in the balance. Cattle ranching has steadily consumed the fragile grasslands this species depends on, and with less than 5% of campo rupestre protected, there is little refuge left. *Canthon corpulentus* reminds us how easily the smallest, least-known lives can be erased before we ever truly knew them.
